M Amirul Islam with SS Halder, MI Farooqui, M Saleem Ullah, M Mohsin Rashid, KM Saifuddin Ahmed, MK Rahman, Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, Shueb Ahmed, Idrisur Rahman, Tania Amir and Shirin Sharmin Chowdhury, Advocates-----For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Wadud Khondker, Additional Attorney-General with Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General with Md. Altafur Rahman, Assistant Attorney-General-----For Respondent No.3.
parties:
Shamsul Huq Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs
Justice Md. Abdur Rouf & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
4. It is stated that the Respondent No.1 joined the High Court Bar on 24-9-65 and the Supreme Court Bar of Pakistan in 1971 and was elevated to the Bench on 29-1-1982 as an Additional Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, High Court Division. The respondent again took oath as a Judge on 26-1-1984. The Respondent No.1 was appointed as the Chief Election Commissioner on 24-12-90 and took oath of office on 25-12-90 as the Chief Election Commissioner. It is stated that after taking oath the Respondent No.1 resigned and/or relinquished his office as a Judge and he continued to hold office as Chief Election Commissioner from 25-12-90 to 18-4-95 but while the tenure of office as Chief Election Commissioner was about to be completed he suddenly relinquished the said office in order to reclaim and resume his old office along with his seniority in the office. On 8-6-1995 the Respondent No. 1 took oath to a new office of the Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and had now been functioning as such in that capacity. 

 5. The first point taken by the petitioner in his application is that as per provision of Article 118(3)(a) of the Constitution, Respondent No.1 having held office as the Chief Election Commissioner is not eligible for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court as the office of a Judge, though a Constitutional office, is an office in the service of the Republic and, as such, they hold office during good behaviour as per Articles 95 and 96 read with Article 147 of the Constitution. 

 6. The second point urged on behalf of the petitioner is that as the Respondent No. 1 once held the Constitutional post of Chief Election Commissioner which is an office of profit in the service of the Republic and having resigned on 18-4-95 as the Chief Election Commissioner is debarred from holding the office as a Judge without fresh appointment and oath and his sitting as a Judge on the concept that he had been in the said office is not compatible with Article 147(3) read with Article 118(3). 

 7. Keeping the above point in view it is argued that there being a Constitutional bar against the respondent No. 1 to hold office of a Judge of the Supreme Court after having held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner the authority of the Respondent No. 1 for holding the office of the Judge of the Appellate Division has triggered controversy and has been challenged by way of writ in the nature of quo-warranto. 

 8. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner, opened his argument with the premises that the Judges of the Supreme Court are in the service of the Republic and in this regard he drew our attention to Article 118(3) (a) and submitted that the Respondent No. 1 having held the office as Chief Election Commissioner shall not be eligible for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court which is an office in the service of the Republic as defined under Article 152 of the Constitution. The learned Counsel also referred to Article 147(3) of the Constitution which provides "no person appointed to or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object." 

 9. It is argued that Respondent No. 1 as the Chief Election Commissioner could not hold the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court relinquishing his office as there is a clear bar under Article 147(3) of the Constitution. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam submitted that the office of a Judge is also a service of the Republic as defined in Article 152 and that being so while the Respondent No.1 having held the office of Chief Election Commissioner for about 4 years cannot come back and sit as a Judge without taking fresh oath and thereafter cannot be appointed a Judge and for that matter hold the office of a Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. He submitted that the State includes Parliament, the Government and statutory public authority according to the defining clause and the Judiciary having not been specifically mentioned therein while defining 'State' it is apparent that the law maker intended to include judiciary within the framework of Government. The learned Counsel submitted that the assumption and or resumption of office as a Judge of the Supreme Court after having continuously served as the Chief Election Commissioner for about four years in violation of Constitutional provision is likely to shake the confidence reposed by the people regarding the independence of judiciary and sanctity, associated with the Constitutional offices of the high order in the Republic, Mr. Islam further elaborated his argument saying that the Respondent while holding the office of a Judge voluntarily accepted the office of the Chief Election Commissioner under different oath under the Constitution and thus having ceased to hold that office as Judge and by virtue of his new and distinct oath under Article 148 of the Constitution was no longer part of the Supreme Court under Article 94 of the Constitution. 

 10. The learned Counsel submitted that the Constitution never contemplates holding of two constitutional posts at a time or to come back to the office of a Judge having a lien as he once held the post of Chief Election Commissioner which was an office of profit in the service of Republic. 

 11. Mr. Abdul Wadud Khondker, the learned Additional Attorney General appearing for the Respondent No. 3, submitted that without seeking declaration to the effect that the appointment of the respondent No. 1 as a Judge of the Appellate Division is without any lawful authority by way of filing application in the nature of certiorari the petitioner cannot challenge the status of the Respondent No. 1 who is not an usurper. In refuting the submission of the learned Counsel for the petitioner the learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court of the either Division is not treated as in the service of the Republic as contemplated under Articles 133-141 of Part IX of the Constitution, the head "Services of Bangladesh" and for that matter the 'Service of the Republic' is distinct and different from the office of Judge and Chief Election Commissioner which are constitutional offices according to the scheme of the constitution. The learned Additional Attorney General pointed out the provision of Articles 94, 95 and 96 of Part VI of the Constitution under the head 'judiciary' which deals with the establishment of the Supreme Court and the appointment of Judges and other matters related there-to. He contended that in respect of the appointment of a judge who once held the office of Chief Election Commissioner the bar imposed under Article 118(3)(a) is not applicable as the Judges are not in the service of the Republic. He submits that the holding of the post of a Judge of the High Court Division, then the post of Chief Election Commissioner and then again resuming his office as the Judge of the High Court Division is a matter of the past and cannot be and, as a matter of fact, has not been challenged in the present writ petition seeking relief therefor, though in the body of the writ petition statements to that effect have been made incidentally. 

 12. In the writ petition though a short back-ground of the respondent No. 1 has been given regarding assumption of office as a Judge of High Court Division and thereafter as Chief Election Commissioner in the prayer while seeking relief the petitioner has confined himself to the point challenging the authority under which the Respondent No.1 has become the Judge of the Appellate Division and has been continuing in such office. 

 16.The learned Counsel contends that Part VI of the Constitution deals with judiciary which remains as a co-ordinate and co-equal organ with the two other organs of the State. The Constitution makers have attached so much importance to the independence of judiciary in this country that they though it necessary to place them beyond all controversy by way of putting the judiciary as one of the three organs of the State. Dialating on the main contention the learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the Respondent No.1 having held that office of the Chief Election Commissioner shall not be eligible for being appointed as the Judge of the Appellate Division because of the limitations and restrictions imposed vide Article 118(3)(a) which runs as follows: 

 (a) a person who has held office as Chief Election Commissioner shall not be eligible for appointment in the service of the Republic." 

 17. Thus Article 118(3)(a) postulates that a person who has ever held the office of Chief Election Commissioner shall not be eligible for appointment in the service of the Republic. Mr. Amirul-Islam argued that the prohibition having been imposed under Article 118(3)(a) and the respondent No. 1 once having held the post of Chief Election Commissioner is not eligible for being appointed as a Judge of the Appellate Division which, according to him, is an appointment in the service of the Republic. Mr. Abdul Wadud Khondker contended that the office of a Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court under no stretch of imagination can be designated as the office in the service of the Republic. Part IX comprising Articles 133-141 of the Constitution provides for the appointment and regulating the conditions of service of the persons in the service of the Republic whereas in Part VI Chapter 1 the Supreme Court and in Chapter II of the said part Subordinate Court have been incorporated. In Article 94 establishment of Supreme Court of Bangladesh with two Divisions, viz Appellate Division and High Court Division, has been provided. In unequivocal terms Article 94 (4) provides that subject to the provision of the Constitution the Chief Justice and the other Judges shall be independent in the exercise of their Judicial functions. The appointments, the qualification for being appointed as Judges and the tenure of office of the Judges have been provided in Article 94 (Establishment of Supreme Court), under Article 95 (Appointment of Judges) Article 96 (Tenure of office of Judge) are distinct and separate from the manner of appointment, qualification and tenure of office of other persons in the service of the Republic as provided under Part IX of the Constitution. In Article 96(i) it is provided that subject to the other provisions of the Article, a Judge shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years, and clause (2) provides that a Judge shall not be removed from office except in accordance with the provisions of clauses (3)(4)(5)(6)(7) and (8) of the said Articles. Referring to the preamble and Article 7 of the Constitution Mr. Amirul-Islam emphasised that all powers belong to the people and the Constitution is the solemn expression of the will of the people, the Supreme Law of the Republic and the fundamental principle of State policy has been enumerated in Part II of the Constitution. Clause (2) of the Article 8 of the Constitution lays down that "the principle set out in this part shall be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh, shall be applied by the state in the making of laws, shall be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and the other laws in Bangladesh and shall be the basis of the works of the State and of its citizens, but shall not be judicially enforceable. "Mr. Islam also referred to Article 22 which reads as "the state shall ensure the separation of judiciary from the executive organ of the state. "There is no controversy with the above submission of Mr. Islam from the side of the respondent Government relating to the above mentioned constitutional provisions. The learned Additional Attorney-General Mr. Wadud Khondker has also laid emphasis on the aforesaid principle. Mr. Islam submitted that though the Constitution emphasises about the fundamental rights of the people, the supremacy of the constitution and the assurance for the separation of Judiciary but, as a matter of fact, this principle has not been followed in the matter of appointing the respondent as Chief Election Commissioner from the position of a Judge of the Supreme Court, High Court Division and then allowing him to come back from the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and to resume his office of the Judge and ultimately appointing him as a Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. 

 18. In this petition as the Rule has been issued in terms of the prayer made in the application on specific point with regard to the appointment of the respondent No.1 as the Judge of the Appellate Division we consider it futile to take up the matters other than the matters in terms of which the Rule has been issued. The learned Counsel for the petitioner has questioned the appointment of the respondent No. 1 as the Judge of the Appellate Division mainly on three grounds: viz (1) the Respondent No. 1 rendered himself ineligible for being appointed as the Judge of the Appellate Division which is an appointment in the service of the Republic as he once held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and thus the Respondent No. 1 Justice Mohammad Abdur Roufs appointment in the office of Judge of the Appellate Division has been made in violation of the provision of law prescribed in clause (3)(a) of Article 118 of the Constitution (ii) the Respondent No. 1 having been appointed and having once held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner to which Article 147 (4)(e)(g) applies, is debarred from holding the office of the Judge of Appellate Division which is an office of profit or emolument iii) there has not been any consultation with the Chief Justice of Bangladesh before the appointment was made and thus there has been breach of the age-old convention. In this petition we have already found that no question has been raised challenging the authority of giving appointment and also about the qualification of the respondent No.1 for being appointed as a Judge of the Appellate Division. The learned Counsel for the petitioner argued that as clause (4) of Article 94 provides that the Judges shall be independent in their functions, and if they are allowed to hold office after they once held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner the sanctity and independence associated with the judicial office becomes questionable. 

 19. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam besides questioning the appointment of the respondent No. 1 on the above mentioned three grounds also reiterated that the appointment is malafide inasmuch as the respondent No. 1 who held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner was allowed to come back and join as the Judge of the High Court Division and then has been taken as the Judge of the Appellate Division in spite of clear prohibition imposed in the Constitution. By referring to the provision of Article 118(3) and other related provisions of the Constitution the learned Counsel submitted that in order to understand and appreciate the bar as created under Article 118(3) of the Constitution it is important to realise the intent and anxiety of the framers of the Constitution underlying the creation of such prohibition attached both to the office of the Chief Election Commissioner as well as to the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court. It is submitted that this bar is of absolute nature with regard to the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and the sitting Judges of the Supreme Court but this has been relaxed only in the case of retired Judges making them eligible for holding the office of the Republic under Article 99 of the Constitution if such offices are of "judicial" or quasi judicial nature. Mr. Islam reiterates that a person who once held office of the Chief Election Commissioner is not eligible for appointment as Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court which is also in the category of the service of the Republic. According to him, this provision has been made in the constitution for ensuring the supremacy of the will of the people and, therefore, it is the sacred duty of every citizen to safeguard, protect and defend the constitution and maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the people of Bangladesh as provided in the preamble read with Articles 7 and 21 of the Constitution. He also submitted that the will of the people has further been expressed by ensuring independence of the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and the Judge of the Supreme Court. It is submitted that this provision carries with it balance in the constitutional governance in order to ensure rule of law and the independence of judiciary. The learned Counsel further submits that a person being in the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and lorthe Judge of the Supreme Court are not only expected to act independently without any fear or favour or influence but also without expectation for any future reward of any kind or in any form as the object and purpose of inserting Article 118(3) in the Constitution is to ensure the independence of both the offices so that each of the offices remain free from any manner of control, influence or expectation of getting the reward. Mr. Islam also referred to the conduct of oath of the Judge which is different and distinct from the one given to the Chief Election Commissioner. He further added that in order to keep the office of the Chief Election Commissioner beyond reproach it was intended to be the last office to be held in the service of the Republic being the last station in life in service. All these arguments of the learned Counsel for the petitioner centred round the conception that the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court and that of the Chief Election Commissioner are in the service of the Republic. By way of elaboration he referred to Article 152 of the Constitution wherein it has been enumerated that" the service of the Republic means a service, post or office whether in civil or military capacity in respect of government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic. "The learned Counsel then submitted that the office of the Chief Election Commissioner and the Judge of the Supreme Court being the office in respect of the Government of Bangladesh falls within the definition of the service of the Republic and that being as the embargo imposed under Article 118(3)(a) is equally applicable in respect of the appointment of the Judges and also the Chief Election Commissioner in their offices and, therefore, if anybody is found to have held the office of the Chief Election Commissioner being in the service of the Republic cannot be allowed to hold the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court which office, according to the learned Counsel, is also in the service of the Republic. Mr. Abdul Wadud Khondker, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.3, contended that the Judge of the either Division of the Supreme Court are not within the perimeter of the service of the Republic and, therefore, prohibition under Article 118(3)(a) is not applicable to the office of the Judges of the Supreme Court at all. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submitted that the terms and conditions relating to the service of the Republic are dealt with in Part IX of the Constitution and this part is distinct and separate from the part VI which deals with the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court for appointing, regulating the terms and conditions of the said office and removal therefrom. It is emphatically asserted by the learned Additional Attorney-General that the office of the Judge is not included in the definition of the service of the Republic. The terms of 'Service of the Republic' as defined under Article 152 included the service, post or office in respect of the Government of Bangladesh but there is no such definition available in the Constitution so as to include the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court in the service of the republic. 

 21.In the Writ Petition No. 37 of 1987 [not reported] the appointment and functioning of Justice AKM Nurul Islam as Vice President was challenged on the ground that he having held the office of Chief Election Commissioner was not eligible to become the Vice President. A Division Bench of the High Court while rejecting the petition summarily in its judgment dated 16-2-87 held as follows: "there is no denial of fact that the respondent was the Chief Election Commissioner before the appointment as Vice President. Now the question whether the office of the Vice President as contemplated in the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as the "Service of the Republic" within the meaning of the term as defined in Article 152 calls for an answer". It is further observed "the term has been defined thus in the article "the service of the Republic" means any service, post or office whether in a civil, military capacity in respect of the Government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic and a person holding or acting in any office of emolument in the service of the Republic is a public office as per definition of this term given in this article." 

 22. The office of the Judges have been dealt with distinctly and separately under Articles 94 to 96 and they have been brought in Article 147(A) which has also clearly distinguished and differentiated the office of the Judge and the Chief Election Commissioner from the office of the person in the Service of the Republic. 

 29. In the case of Union of India vs. Sankalch and Nimatal Shoth and another reported in AIR 1971 (SC) 2328 it was found "on the other question the rejection of Mr. Seervail's arguments that a High Court Judge cannot be transferred without his consent, should not be read as a negation of his argument that there is no master and servant relationship between the Government and High Court Judges." Thus, there is a fundamental distinction between the master and .servant relationship as is generally understood 'and the relationship between the Government and High Court Judges. They, the Judges of the High Court, are not Government servants in the ordinary signification of that expression'. From the specific provision made in Part VI of the Constitution regarding Ute procedure of appointing the Judges of the Supreme Court regulating their service conditions and tenure of office, removable only under the procedure laid down in Articles 49-99 in Part VI of the Constitution without mentioning anywhere as to whether the said office is in the service of the Republic and the separate and distinct procedure having been laid down under Articles 133-139 in Part IX of the Constitution regarding the appointment and condition of service, tenure of office of the person in the employment of the service of Bangladesh specifically mentioning the services of those persons as in the services of Bangladesh, the learned Additional Attorney-General argued that since the office of the Judge or the Chief Election Commissioner is not in the service of the Republic the legislature in its wisdom has not contemplated to include the Judges of the Supreme Court in the service of the Republic under Articles 133-139 of Part IX of the Constitution but has placed the offices of the Judges under the head judiciary as a separate organ of the State as under Articles 96-99 of the Constitution. It is submitted that the office of the Judges and the Chief Election Commissioner and the terms and conditions of service and the mode of appointment and removal of the Judges and the Chief Election Commissioner have been provided under distinct and separate heads. The service of Republic as defined under Article 152 does not include the office of the Judges and the Election Commissioners. It is also argued 'that Republic of' Bangladesh and Government of Bangladesh convey two different meanings and the Constitution provides the "Supreme Court of Bangladesh and not 'Supreme Court of the Government of Bangladesh. 

 31. Having regard to the discussion made above and the constitutional set-up we do not find any reasonable ground to hold that office of the Judge is in the service of the Republic which has been specifically enumerated in the Articles 133-139 of Part IX of our Constitution under the head "The Services of Bangladesh and, therefore, holding of the office of the Chief Election Commissioner by the Respondent No. 1, in our view, has not, created any bar in the appointment of Justice Mohammad Abdur Rouf as a Judge of the, Appellate Division of the Supreme Court While summing up his argument Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned counsel for the petitioner, placed his last trump card submitting that Justice Roufs appointment as a Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court is a fresh one and not in continuation of the office held by him earlier as a Judge of the High Court Division and as such consultation with the Chief Justice before his appointment was imperative and in the absence of such consultation the appointment has been rendered invalid. 

 32. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned counsel for the petitioner, could not deny that after the Fourth Amendment now there does not exist any constitutional requirement for the appointing authority to have consultation with the Chief Justice before appointing a Judge but since a convention has grown up due to the time-old practice followed since 1862 in the matter of appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court consultation with the Chief Justice is a necessary prerequisite and, therefore in the absence of such consultation fundamental principle of independence of judiciary as enshrined in our Constitution cannot be ensured. In reply, the learned Attorney General submitted that this argument of the counsel for the petitioner is of no avail as the petitioner on the ground that consultation clause has since been omitted by Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act 1975 (Act 11 of 1975) and furthermore the petitioner has neither challenged the Fourth Amendment nor the Eleventh Amendment in the petition and, as such, no Rule was prayed for and issued in the said terms. 

 33. Mr. Wadud Khondker, the learned Additional Attorney-General, further submitted that the argument of the Counsel for the petitioner giving emphasis on the consultation is wholly speculative and untenable in as much as the consultation by the appointing authority with the Chief Justice before appointing a Judge is neither a constitutional requirement nor it has ripened into a convention and, in that view of the matter, appointment of the Respondent No.1 cannot be held unauthorised, unconstitutional and, as such, invalid. The learned Additional Attorney-General added that consultation before appointment of a Judge of the Supreme Court is a privileged communication between the appointing authority and the learned Chief Justice and in the above context the learned Chief Justice having already administered oath of office of Justice Mohammad Abdur Rouf as the Judge of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh the question whether there was consultation Of not cannot be raised at this stage. Even in India where consultation with 'the Chief Justice by the appointing authority has been incorporated as an essential prerequisite in the Constitution before appointing a Judge of the superior courts, the Supreme Court of India in the case of SP Gupta and others vs. President of India and others reported in AIR 1982 (SC) page 149 relevant page 199 paras 28 & 29 while dealing with the matter of consultation has gone to the extent of making observation that consultation does not mean concurrence.
